name: Uma Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the repair crew for the farm district around Wheatley, flat country, miles of wheat and long straight roads. A lot of what we do is lines brought down by storms, tractors clipping a pole, or lightning taking out a transformer. We start at the depot at seven, and if there's a fault the call can come any time. In summer the storms roll across the plain and you can watch them coming for an hour before they hit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Getting a farm's power back on. When the milking machines have stopped and you see the farmer's face when it comes back, that's worth the mud. I've got an apprentice now, Jess, twenty-two, and I like teaching her. She reminds me of me at that age, too quick and too sure.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Glen, my husband, hurt his back at the tractor factory five years ago and gets a small disability pension, so I'm the main wage. We've got two acres with hens and a vegetable patch, and two grown children, both married. A hailstorm took our roof last spring and the insurance didn't cover all of it, so we're down to about two weeks of money. The pay here's less than in town, and there's no other line work out on the plain. I sing in the church choir on Sundays, that's my rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can stop worrying and get on with the work. I use it now and then to tidy up the church newsletter, and that's about the size of it. I'd say that at the depot and after choir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep going to sixty-six and Glen and I get by. Nothing fancy, but nothing scary either. I'd rather worry about hail than about computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal. Sell a few more eggs at the gate, maybe start doing jam again for the church fair, to rebuild after the roof. And keep teaching Jess, because she'll be running the crew one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet evening after a storm's passed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use the AI for the newsletter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I write it the way I talk, which is all over the place, and ask it to make it neat. Then I put back the bits it took out, because it makes everything sound like a bank letter. Pastor Dale says it reads better now, so I keep doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Glen's back, and money if another storm takes the shed. We're one bad month from the credit card. That's got nothing to do with computers.

S0.say: I'd say good, now we can stop worrying and get on with the work, since I only use AI to tidy the church newsletter. I'd say that at the depot and after choir.
S0.think: It means I keep going to sixty-six and Glen and I get by, nothing fancy and nothing scary. I'd rather worry about hail than about computers.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and sells more eggs at the gate and jam at the church fair to rebuild after the roof repair. Keeps training her apprentice to run the crew one day.
S0.feel: Calm, like a quiet evening after a storm.
S0.quote: I'd rather worry about hail than about computers.
S0.fieldNote: Uma is the main earner since her husband's injury, which makes her careful with money. She uses AI now and then and puts back what it takes out of her writing. Her small farm gives her a little extra income and a lot of steadiness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses will work it out, they always do. If it makes the job safer and the company more efficient, fine, as long as they keep training people. I'd say the market will sort the good tools from the bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I worry about Jess more than me. If they start using drones and software to find faults, they'll need fewer of us, and the youngest go first. I've got eight years. She's got forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see which tools actually work, then learn them, the way I did with the fault-finding meter. I'd make sure Jess learns them first, because she'll pick them up faster and she'll need them longer. And I'd keep the eggs and jam going, a bit more seriously, to put something aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but thinking about it on long drives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the market will sort it out. Do you believe that for people too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For businesses, yes. For people, it's not the market that sorts it, it's families and churches and neighbours. I've seen that out here when the factory cut jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the factory cut jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Glen's friends were laid off at fifty-five. The ones who did all right had family nearby and the church behind them. The ones on their own drifted, and two of them never really worked again.

S1.say: I'd say businesses always work it out, and new tools are fine if they make the job safer and the company keeps training people. The market will sort the good tools from the bad.
S1.think: I worry about my apprentice more than me, because fewer crew would be needed and the youngest go first. I've got eight years and she's got forty.
S1.do: Waits to see which tools work, then learns them, making sure her apprentice learns them first. Takes egg and jam sales more seriously to put something aside.
S1.feel: Uneasy, thinking it over on long drives.
S1.quote: For people, it's not the market that sorts it, it's families and churches and neighbours.
S1.fieldNote: Uma trusts markets for businesses but not for people, drawing on what she saw when her husband's factory cut jobs. Her concern is mainly for her young apprentice. She adopts tools once they're proven, as she did with the fault-finding meter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to pull together, as families and towns, because two years is too fast for anyone. I wouldn't be calling for a big government scheme, they'd make a mess of it. But I'd want the company to do right by its people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be sixty, the only real wage in the house, with two weeks of savings. If the job goes, Glen's pension won't pay the bills. I'd be frightened, I won't pretend otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, cut everything but the bills and food, and grow more of our own. Glen could manage the hens and veg properly, and we'd sell at the Saturday market in town. I'd ask the church about any help for families in trouble, and our kids would chip in if we asked. And I'd take whatever redundancy or early retirement they offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd wake at three in the morning and go out to the hens just to do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having two years' warning help at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Two years is enough time to build up the market stall and get the vegetable patch producing properly. It's not enough to save money or learn a new trade on my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jess?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to look for something else while she's young, maybe the robot side. It would break my heart, I've put two years into her. But I'd rather she left than got stuck.

S2.say: I'd say we need to pull together as families and towns because two years is too fast for anyone. I wouldn't call for a big government scheme, but I'd want the company to do right by its people.
S2.think: I'd be sixty, the main wage in the house, with two weeks of savings, and Glen's pension won't cover the bills. I'd be frightened, I won't pretend otherwise.
S2.do: Cuts spending to bills and food, grows more food and sets up a Saturday market stall with her husband. Asks the church and her children for help and takes any redundancy or early retirement offered.
S2.feel: Alarmed, waking at three in the morning.
S2.quote: I'd wake at three in the morning and go out to the hens just to do something.
S2.fieldNote: As the main earner with almost no savings, Uma is alarmed by the fast scenario. Her answer is family, church and the small farm rather than government schemes. Telling her apprentice to leave the trade would hurt her deeply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to prepare, so families and businesses should get on with it. Train the young ones, look after the older ones. I'd say it after choir and at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three. That's close to the pension, and if I can hold on, we'd manage. It's three years of a gap, not six, and with the stall and the hens we might bridge it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build up the market stall over the first two years so it's a real income by the time the job goes. I'd learn any new tools once they're proven, to stay useful longer. And I'd start saving fifty a month, whatever it costs us in treats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'd have something to work towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build the stall slowly, the right way. In two years I'd be scrambling. In five, I could have a proper stall with regulars by the time I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Glen be up to running the stall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some days. His back is bad in the cold. But he likes talking to people, and he's better with customers than I am. I'd do the heavy lifting on weekends.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to prepare, so families and businesses should get on with it, training the young and looking after the old. I'd say it after choir and at the depot.
S3.think: I'd be sixty-three, close to the pension, with a three-year gap rather than six. With the stall and the hens we might bridge it.
S3.do: Builds the market stall over the first two years into a real income and learns proven new tools to stay useful longer. Saves fifty a month, cutting out treats.
S3.feel: Anxious, with something to work towards.
S3.quote: He likes talking to people, and he's better with customers than I am.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Uma turn the small farm into a real bridge to her pension. She pictures her husband running the stall despite his back. She'd keep learning tools to stay useful a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for families or companies not to be ready. Get the young ones into apprenticeships for whatever's coming. I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-eight, retired, with the hens and the choir. It's Jess and my grandchildren I'd think about. I'd be fine, I think, if I've saved a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work to sixty-six, keep the stall going for extra, save a little each month. Help Jess get onto any new training the company offers. Talk to my children about what their kids should study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'if I've saved a bit'. How sure are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very. Every time we get ahead, something happens, the roof, Glen's back. But ten years is a long time, and the stall would help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your grandchildren to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something useful with their hands as well as their heads. And I'd want them to stay near family. That's what gets people through.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so families and companies have no excuse not to be ready. Get the young ones into apprenticeships for whatever is coming.
S4.think: I'd be sixty-eight and retired, with the hens and the choir, and fine if I've saved a bit. I'd think about my apprentice and my grandchildren.
S4.do: Works to sixty-six, keeps the market stall for extra income and saves a little each month. Helps her apprentice onto new training and talks with her children about what their kids should study.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, mostly for the young.
S4.quote: Every time we get ahead, something happens, the roof, Glen's back.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Uma's own timeline looks safe on paper, but she doubts her saving plans because of past setbacks. She stays focused on her apprentice and grandchildren. Staying near family is her main advice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is the company keeping people near retirement on until the pension, and keeping the apprenticeships going for the young. And churches and towns getting organised to help families, because that works better than forms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the farms. When the power goes out here, the cows still need milking. Whoever fixes the lines, machine or person, they'd better come quick.

headlineQuote: When the power goes out here, the cows still need milking.
portrait: Uma Tanaka is a fifty-eight-year-old repair-crew lineworker in flat farm country, and the main earner since her husband hurt his back at a tractor factory. A hailstorm left them with about two weeks of savings, and they keep hens and vegetables on two acres. She sings in the church choir, uses AI now and then for the church newsletter, and trusts markets for businesses but families and churches for people. She is calm when AI fizzles, uneasy for her apprentice under steady change and alarmed by AGI in two years. With more time she plans to turn the small farm into a market stall that bridges her to the pension.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she's the main wage with two weeks of savings and her husband's pension wouldn't cover the bills.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping people near retirement on until their pension, keeping apprenticeships going, and churches and towns organising to help families.
